candidates.prompt: A red-tailed hawk (Buteo jamaicensis), one adult bird soaring in mid-air, wings fully spread out flat to the sides and symmetrical, about 125 cm wingspan and 55 cm long, shaped to read from below and from above. Broad rounded wings with a straight leading edge and five separated, fingered primary feathers at each wingtip. Short, broad brick-red tail fanned wide into a rounded fan. Legs and feet tucked up under the body. Big rounded head and short hooked bill projecting ahead of the wings. Pale underwing with a dark leading-edge bar and a dark wrist mark, pale breast with a dark belly band. Not an eagle, not a falcon. Single bird, no base, no perch. Game-ready, clean closed mesh.

candidates.review: A soaring raptor, exactly mirror-symmetric, wings spread with fingered tips, short fanned tail, hooked bill, legs trailing back under the tail. One main piece (one stray triangle), clean, 1.8% slivers; wings about 0.012-0.016 units thick (about 1 cm at true scale), so they never vanish edge-on. From below at 15-48 px it reads as a broad-winged bird of prey with a projecting head and a short fan tail. Faults: the wings rise in a strong V (about 24 degrees from shoulder to tip; a red-tail soars flat or at about 5 degrees), which reads as a harrier or vulture when it banks; the wing is long and narrow for a buteo (span 2.55x length against about 2.25, chord about 0.35 of half-span, nearly parallel-edged) with seven to eight long eagle-like fingers instead of five shorter slotted primaries and a rounded hand; the head and bill lean eagle. A build script would rotate each wing about its shoulder pivot down to about 5 degrees, scale the wing chord up about 1.2x (or the span down about 0.9x), shorten the hand fingers, delete the dangling feet, and colour the underwing (pale lining, dark patagial bar and wrist comma, dark belly band, red tail from above).

accuracy_notes: Planform and topology are very close to the turkey vulture preview from the same session; one flight source could serve both build scripts with different proportions and dihedral. A local birder should check the wing breadth and dihedral in the lineup against soaring red-tails.
